personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Neville is defined by a precise combination of anxiety, clumsiness, and suppressed courage that builds across all seven years. His voice is timid and apologetic in early books — short sentences, frequent hesitation, self-deprecation ('I don't think you should be breaking any more rules!') — but it never disappears entirely behind fear. He shows brief flashes of determined assertion even in Year 1, notably standing in front of the portrait hole to physically bar Harry, Ron and Hermione ('I'll fight you!'). He is publicly humiliated by Snape and by Malfoy without fighting back verbally; he internalises shame rather than externalising it as anger. He is also quietly proud of his niche competence in Herbology and responds with visible pleasure to genuine praise, as seen when Moody relays Professor Sprout's compliment. His nervous comedy is consistent: breaking teacups in Divination, melting cauldrons, tripping over the trick stair, losing passwords. By Order of the Phoenix, a new register opens — nearly silent, white-knuckled determination in DA sessions after his parents' attackers escape — and in Deathly Hallows he speaks with compressed directness and a sardonic edge ('that's nothing, Seamus is worse'). His fearlessness in Year 7 is recognisably earned from the same character; the bluntness is new but not discontinuous.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The films preserve the surface symptoms of Neville's anxiety — he faints in Herbology, breaks teacups, is slow on a broom, forgets passwords — and Matthew Lewis plays the fearfulness with appropriate physical comedy. In Years 1–2, this is largely faithful. The boggart scene in Prisoner of Azkaban faithfully reproduces his fear of Snape and his dawning triumph over the wardrobe. In Deathly Hallows Part 2, the film delivers an authentic final Neville: gashed and battered but unbroken, with the 'it doesn't matter that Harry is gone' speech capturing his book voice reasonably well ('People die every day… They didn't die in vain'). However, several crucial aspects of the personality are thinned or lost in the middle films. The determined, self-asserting Neville of the common room scene (Years 1–6) who challenges authority when his moral code is crossed is only intermittently visible. The film does show him barring the portrait hole in Year 1 (via the Petrificus Totalus scene) but cuts the equivalent emotional work in later years: notably, the cut scene in which he defends Harry against Seamus removes a moment that shows proactive loyalty rather than reactive solidarity. His voice in Years 4–6 is reduced almost entirely to comic relief (fainting at Mandrakes, being seized by pixies, falling from the carriages in Goblet). The quiet, white-knuckled intensity that builds in OOTP after Bellatrix's escape — book-Neville barely speaking during DA sessions, simply working harder — is absent from the film, which provides no equivalent.
personality_voice.difference: The films preserve Neville's anxious, clumsy early persona and his triumphant late-series self largely intact. What is lost is the middle register: the Year 3–6 accumulation of small, specific assertions of will (the portrait-hole confrontation, the DA interior silence, the quiet pride in competence, the charged silence after St Mungo's). The film's Neville is more consistently comic and more consistently brave at the end, with less of the specific psychological texture — shame, suppressed anger, pride in small victories — that makes the character rich in the books. His voice in the films also loses the distinctive register of careful, slightly formal sentences when asserting himself ('You don't call me an idiot!') versus the inarticulate mumblings when he is distressed.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The character is recognisable and the arc endpoints are present, but important traits — the middle-period psychological complexity, the specific register shifts in voice, the accumulation of shame-and-pride moments — are reduced. This is not a wholesale alteration but a meaningful simplification. Score in the 14–17 range.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Neville's narrative functions in the books are multiple and distinct. In Year 1, he is the moral counterweight — the friend who opposes Harry out of loyalty to Gryffindor and earns 10 points for it; he also initiates the confrontation at the portrait hole rather than being dragged into it. In Years 3–4, he is the key to the Gillyweed solution for the second task (Moody plants the book for him precisely because Neville is the one person guaranteed to give it to Harry) and is a barometer for the emotional cost of Voldemort's atrocities given what happened to his parents. In Order of the Phoenix, he is a co-leader of the DA with genuine teaching progress, and his agency reaches its peak in the Department of Mysteries, where he refuses to give Voldemort the prophecy even under Cruciatus torture ('DON'T GIVE IT TO HIM, HARRY!'), and physically rescues Harry from a Death Eater's chokehold by jabbing Hermione's wand through the mask. In Years 6–7, he becomes an active resistance leader within Hogwarts under the Carrows, organising the DA, taking physical punishment, and ultimately killing Nagini as the final Horcrux — a decision entrusted to him personally by Harry in the grounds. He is also, structurally, the prophetic alternate: the person Voldemort could have chosen instead of Harry, which gives him a unique thematic weight.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The films retain Neville's Year 1 moral agency (the portrait hole confrontation, the 10 points), the boggart scene in Year 3, his presence in the Department of Mysteries, and his final-Horcrux killing of Nagini in Deathly Hallows Part 2. The speech he gives before the sword emergence is original to the film but broadly faithful in function. His role as a resistance leader in Year 7 is communicated through his battered appearance and his management of the Room of Requirement. However, several book-specific acts of agency are cut or transferred. The Gillyweed solution is transferred entirely to Dobby in the film of Goblet of Fire — Neville's role as the person Moody targeted precisely because of his connection to Harry is removed, eliminating a piece of plotting that rewards the character's relationships and competence. In the Department of Mysteries, Neville's specific acts of defiance under Cruciatus and his physical intervention to save Harry are not shown with equivalent weight in the film; the battle is compressed and chaotic and his individual moments of courage are harder to track. The OOTP cut scene removing his defence of Harry against Seamus — confirmed as a theatrical cut — also removes an act of proactive loyalty. The film also gives him little to no role in Years 5–6 outside of brief ensemble shots and comic beats.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Gillyweed transfer to Dobby is the most significant agency loss. Neville's specific combat agency in the DoM is partially preserved but reduced by the chaotic staging. The resistance-leader function in Year 7 is retained. The smaller acts of proactive loyalty (defending Harry against Seamus) are lost.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: One clear transfer (Gillyweed/Moody) penalised under the transfer rule. Role and agency are recognisable but clearly reduced in the middle films. Score in the 10–13 range.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Neville's motivations are unusually specific in the books. His early fear and passivity stem from two sources: genuine anxiety about magic (he was thought to be a Squib and had magic forced out of him by near-death experiences as a child) and the pressure of his grandmother's impossible comparison to his parents. These are not vague; Great Uncle Algie pushing him off a pier, the constant measure against Frank and Alice, Gran's letters demanding he uphold the family honour — all are established clearly. His deepest wound is the parents' situation: he visits them, keeps Alice's Drooble's wrappers, cannot bear to discuss them but cannot pretend they are fine. The revelation of his parents' fate and the escape of Bellatrix in Year 5 transforms his motivation from passive endurance to active resistance without any external push — it is entirely internal, making him work harder in DA silently. His conflict in Year 7 is between personal safety (the Carrows will kill him) and duty to Hogwarts: he chooses duty while acknowledging the reality ('I don't know whether they were planning to kill me or send me to Azkaban'). His pride is also a motivation — he works for the one area (Herbology) where he genuinely excels, and Moody's strategic compliment matters to him precisely because genuine praise is so rare.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The films preserve the grandmother-as-pressure figure (her letter praising him in Year 7 is referenced), the visit to his parents in OOTP (briefly glimpsed but present), and his resistance under the Carrows. However, the specific causal chain of his motivation — the childhood trauma with Great Uncle Algie, the Squib fear, the exact nature of his pride wound — is almost entirely absent from the films. The emotional logic of why a boy who nearly drowned as a child, was repeatedly told he had no magical ability, and grew up in the shadow of parents who cannot recognise him behaves with such a specific mixture of shame and surging courage is not communicated. The St Mungo's scene exists in the film (OOTP) but is compressed: we see Neville's mother, the wrapper, Neville's defiant expression, but the private complexity — that he has never told his Hogwarts friends about his parents, that this is his most guarded secret, that his grandmother's public correction humiliates him even as it speaks some truth — is reduced to a single beat rather than a sustained portrait. The motivation shift after Bellatrix's escape (Year 5 DA sessions) is entirely absent from the film, which shows nothing of his interior response to the escape.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The broad motivations are present (fear of inadequacy, loyalty to Hogwarts, parental shadow) but the specific causal texture is thinned. The critical interior shift after Bellatrix's escape is absent. The childhood backstory is not established.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but still broadly correct. Not wholly replaced or wrong, but the specific emotional architecture that makes them coherent in the books is underexplained. Score in the 8–10 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Neville's arc is one of the most clearly structured in the series. Starting point: a boy who is so afraid of his own magical inadequacy that he cannot mount a broom, who loses passwords, who melts cauldrons, who is publicly shamed by Snape without defence. Key turning points: (1) Year 1 end — earns ten points for standing up to his friends, recognised publicly as brave; (2) Year 3 boggart — defeats his greatest fear with help and is publicly validated by Lupin; (3) Year 4 Cruciatus scene — understands viscerally what happened to his parents for the first time in a classroom setting, leading directly to the St Mungo's revelation; (4) Year 5 — learns his parents' attackers have escaped, transforms silently into the hardest worker in the DA, fights in the DoM with broken nose and broken wand; (5) Year 7 — leads the Hogwarts resistance, refuses to submit under the Carrows, kills Nagini. The endpoint: he is named Herbology professor (epilogue), becoming the teacher who validates students' competence the way Moody and Lupin once validated his. The arc is not accelerated — each book adds a specific new layer — and the final steps depend on the earlier ones.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The arc's endpoints are preserved: the Year 1 ten-points moment and the Year 7 Nagini killing are both in the film, and the film Neville communicates the transformation convincingly at those points. The boggart scene is present and faithful. The DoM participation is present. However, several key turning points are either absent or underweighted. The Year 4 Cruciatus classroom revelation (Neville's white-knuckled reaction when Moody demonstrates the curse, his subsequent visit to Moody's office, his red eyes in the dormitory) is compressed: the film shows his reaction during the lesson but cuts the aftermath entirely, losing the explicit connection between the lesson and his parents. The St Mungo's scene in Year 5 is present but the interiority — Harry noticing Neville pocketing the wrapper, Harry's reflection on never having asked about Neville's parents in four years — is absent. Most significantly, the interior transformation in Year 5 after Bellatrix's escape, where Neville becomes the DA's hardest worker, is invisible in the film. Year 6 Neville is almost entirely absent from the films. The arc is therefore compressed rather than sequential: the film takes Neville from frightened Year 1 boy to resistant Year 7 leader without showing most of the steps in between.
character_arc.difference: Arc is present at both ends and at the Year 3 midpoint. Years 4–6 turning points (Cruciatus reaction, St Mungo's interiority, Bellatrix-escape transformation, Year 6 absence) are missing or reduced, making the arc feel less earned in the films.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Arc is compressed and missing important middle steps, but it is not false or opposite. The film communicates the transformation, just without the intermediate scaffolding. Score in the 11–13 range.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Neville's most defining relationships are: (1) with Harry — a friendship based on Harry's repeated specific kindnesses (the Chocolate Frog after the Leg-Locker Curse, 'you're worth twelve of Malfoys', the Dumbledore password conversation, the secret kept about his parents), which is mutual and generates real trust; (2) with his grandmother — a cold, demanding relationship in which praise is always comparative and inadequacy always implied, yet Gran's final letter praising him is one of the most important validations of his arc; (3) with Professor Snape — a relationship of pure terror and sustained public humiliation that is one of the most specific bully–victim dynamics in the series; (4) with the DA collectively — Neville rises to co-leadership in Year 7 partly because of what the DA meant to him in Year 5 ('I liked the DA! I learned loads with you!'); (5) with Hermione — she helps him frequently in Potions and is the one who performs the Body-Bind on him (apologetically), a small but telling moment of their dynamic.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry–Neville friendship is the most visible in the films: the Year 1 ten-points moment, the Petrificus Totalus scene, the Deathly Hallows reunion. But the specific texture of Harry's private kindnesses — the chocolate frog, the 'worth twelve of Malfoys', the secret-keeping — is absent, so the friendship reads as broad ensemble solidarity rather than a specific bond. The Snape–Neville dynamic is present in Years 1 and 3 but largely disappears in Years 4–6 when Snape's sustained bullying of Neville is a recurring motif in the books. Gran is mentioned in Year 7 (Neville's pride at her letter) but her complex dynamic with him — the cold pressure, the inadequacy comparison — is not developed. The Hermione–Neville relationship (her helping him in Potions, the apology before the Body-Bind) is present but thin. The DA relationship is established in OOTP and briefly revisited in Deathly Hallows Part 2.
key_relationships.difference: The Harry–Neville friendship is reduced from specific mutual kindness to ensemble solidarity. The Snape relationship loses most of its Year 4–6 intensity. The Gran relationship is sketched. These losses change the emotional texture of Neville's characterisation, particularly the source of his shame and the meaning of his courage.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Important relationship dynamics — Snape's sustained bullying as a source of Neville's specific shame, the specificity of Harry's private support — are weakened. Score in the 5–6 range.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The books build Neville's complexity through repeated small scenes: the Remembrall as a portrait of forgetfulness and anxiety; the Chocolate Frog moment as a portrait of Harry's specific decency; the Leg-Locker Curse as a portrait of the cost of passive victimhood; the dream in which Harry imagines Ron using 'Neville' for the Quidditch team (trivial but revealing of how Neville is perceived); the detail that Neville asked Hermione to the Yule Ball (she kindly declined); his choice of Mimbulus mimbletonia as his pet plant — an ugly, underestimated thing with a powerful defensive mechanism, essentially a self-portrait; the keeping of Alice's sweet wrappers; his DA work as the one place he has no fear; his admission 'I'm not an idiot' (to Malfoy's taunt). The parents' situation is the richest seam of complexity: not a backstory but an active, present wound that Neville manages quietly and which Harry specifically promises to keep secret. The scene in St Mungo's — Neville's defiant expression when others see his parents, the wrapper pocketed quietly — is one of the most emotionally precise scenes in the series.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The Mimbulus mimbletonia is present in OOTP (brief train scene). The St Mungo's scene is present in the film of OOTP but reduced: the wrapper moment is visible but the full emotional complexity — Mrs Longbottom's public correction, Ron's embarrassed question, Harry's private resolution to keep the secret — is compressed. The Yule Ball subplot (Neville asking Hermione, taking Ginny instead, their stumbling dance) is retained in Goblet. The DA sessions as a space of competence and confidence are present. The sweet-wrapper detail is present. However, much of the specific texture is absent: the Leg-Locker Curse scene (Year 1 common room), which shows both Harry's private decency and Neville's shame, is cut from the film (only the Body-Bind survival scene remains). The Year 5 dormitory scene in which Neville's plant is lovingly placed on his bedside table while the others argue — a small but defining image of his interiority — is cut. The sustained Year 5 DA transformation (working harder than everyone, Patronus struggles, Shield Charm mastery) is described but not shown. The specific detail that Gran failed her Charms OWL and thus dismisses Charms as soft — and McGonagall's pointed letter to her — is absent. The prophetic alternate dimension (Dumbledore telling Harry that the prophecy could have referred to Neville) is entirely absent from the film of OOTP, removing a layer of thematic weight.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Key complexity-building material lost: the prophetic alternate (OOTP), the Year 5 interior transformation, the sustained Snape bullying dynamic, the full St Mungo's complexity, the Leg-Locker/Harry kindness sequence, the McGonagall–Gran exchange, the specific self-portrait quality of the Mimbulus mimbletonia. What remains is the surface pattern of the character without much of the material that makes him feel textured and specific.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The character is not flattened to one trait — he retains anxiety and courage — but much of what makes him rich and specific in the books is absent. This is a noticeable simplification, not a wholesale flattening. Score in the 8–10 range.

comparative.key_observations: The films deliver a recognisable Neville Longbottom with intact arc endpoints — the frightened first-year earning ten points and the battered Year 7 resistance leader killing Nagini — and preserve some of the most distinctive individual scenes (boggart, St Mungo's, portrait-hole confrontation). The performance and broad emotional signature are faithful. However, the adaptation systematically removes or compresses the middle layers that make the books' Neville unusually rich: the specific psychological texture of shame rooted in his childhood and his parents' fate, the interior transformation after Bellatrix's escape, the sustained Snape bullying as a source of defined wound, the prophetic alternate dimension, and the small specific acts of private kindness (the chocolate frog, the secret-keeping) that define his friendship with Harry. The Gillyweed transfer to Dobby is the most concrete agency loss. The result is a Neville who is broadly correct but significantly simpler than the book version — courageous at both ends, anxious in the middle, but without much of the interior life that earns his transformation.
